html:
The Wars of the Diadochi, "successors", were the wars fought among the generals of Alexander the Great after his death in 323 BCE. In about forty years of fighting they broke his empire into rival kingdoms.

Alexander left no adult heir. At the Partition of Babylon his officers shared out the provinces, with Perdiccas as regent, but he was murdered by his own officers in 321 BCE. Alexander's mother Olympias, his half-brother and his young son were all killed in the struggle. In 306 BCE the generals began to call themselves kings.

The main players:

  • Antigonus the One-Eyed held Anatolia and Syria in the largest kingdom; his son Demetrius laid the famous siege of Rhodes in 305 BCE.
  • Cassander ruled Macedon and Greece.
  • Lysimachus held Thrace.
  • Ptolemy held Egypt and Seleucus held Babylon and the east.

The others joined against Antigonus and killed him at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. Seleucus beat Lysimachus at Corupedium in 281 BCE but was murdered soon after. Three dynasties came out of it: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia and the Antigonids in Macedon.
